clue.text: Underwear worn by two thieves, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the phrase is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a nicker is British slang for a thief, one who nicks things, and two make a pair

explanation.surface: A pair of burglars caught wearing the stolen lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: To nick is British slang for to steal, so a nicker is a thief; the silent K is the only difference in sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Knickers are women's underpants, and a single garment is conventionally called a pair.

clue.text: Easy pickings, only poor fed more wretchedly

indicators.note: something done wretchedly is done badly, so the letters come out in a botched order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: The poor are fed more badly and make easy targets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Easy pickings' looks like it describes the poor; it is the definition of a British idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes income earned for almost no effort, which is what easy pickings means.

clue.text: Draught of a freezing drink

blocks.note: bitter weather is freezing cold
a common alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Sounds like an order for an ice-cold drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a hoppy British ale, usually served on draught from the pump.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught here is beer drawn from a cask, and bitter is the classic British pub example.

clue.text: A reception that's appreciated

blocks.note: first meaning: a noun for the greeting a guest is given
second meaning: an adjective for something gladly received

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about a pleasant reception, but it holds a noun and an adjective sense of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the greeting offered on arrival, and the adjective describes anything gladly received or wanted.

clue.text: Tone of European Union accepting credit

indicators.note: whatever accepts something takes it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: A political comment on the mood of Brussels as it takes on debt.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is a pale greyish-yellow shade, so it is a colour tone of fabric or paint.

clue.text: Pluck the student out and get his other name

blocks.note: surface reading: remove a learner from a course or a class

blocks.clueFragment: Pluck the student out and get his other name
blocks.note: setter's reading: drop the L for learner from the word pluck to leave the name of a mischievous sprite, then give his alternative name

explanation.surface: Someone is pulled out of school and asked for a different name.
explanation.walkthrough: PLUCK without L (learner driver's plate, so student) is PUCK, the fairy of A Midsummer Night's Dream, who is also called ROBIN GOODFELLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: In English folklore and Shakespeare the hobgoblin Puck is also known by an alternative title as a household spirit.

clue.text: Presumption is a bit like Gert 'n Daisy without Daisy, unfortunately

indicators.note: going without something means it is left out, so that name is struck from the phrase
things that turn out unfortunately go wrong, so the remaining letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.clueFragment: is a bit like Gert 'n Daisy
blocks.note: taken as written; Gert and Daisy were a British comedy double act of the wartime era

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a solo act is presumptuous without its partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The double act's name is quoted so the second half can be removed; what is left, including the 'n, is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking liberties is behaving with too much familiarity or boldness, which is what presumption means.

clue.text: Work goes back and forth on location? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: going forth and then back means the word is written once forwards and then once from its end to its start

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a musical work, going forth
the same abbreviation again, this time going back
a site is a location

explanation.surface: A question about work shuttling to and fro on location, then a contrary remark.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the wordplay; 'Quite the reverse' is a whole phrase serving as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'quite the reverse' asserts the contrary is true, and contrary is a sense of the answer.

clue.text: Church examination related to singing

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for church
an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: A test for church choristers.
explanation.definitionFit: Choral describes music sung by a choir, so it pertains to vocal performance by groups.

clue.text: Entertain a bird to tea, say

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word and keep only what it sounds like

blocks.note: a diver is a waterbird, the loon
the letter T is pronounced like the drink

explanation.surface: Hosting a bird for afternoon tea.
explanation.definitionFit: To divert someone is to amuse or distract them, a slightly old-fashioned synonym for entertaining.

clue.text: I organise credit union with a hundred before getting cross

indicators.note: before tells us the group of pieces just listed comes earlier in the line than the opening pair

blocks.note: accounting abbreviation
common abbreviation
Roman numeral
taken as written
to fix something is to arrange it

explanation.surface: A union official organising credit ends up angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I organise' comes first in the clue but last in the grid, because 'before' moves the credit-union group ahead of it. 'Cross' looks like angry; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A crucifix is a cross bearing the figure of Christ, so it is a specific religious cross.

clue.text: Nothing included for turning back top

indicators.note: something included is placed within another, so one piece goes inside
turning back means the combined letters are read from the end to the start

blocks.note: taken as written
zero, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: Someone excluded from consideration when changing their mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A roof is the covering on the upper side of a building, so it is the top of it.

clue.text: Got a merger arranged to get another loan

indicators.note: things arranged are put into a new order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A company arranges a merger in order to refinance.
explanation.definitionFit: To remortgage is to take out a fresh home loan against the same property, often to release cash.

clue.text: A board of equals?

blocks.note: surface reading: a committee or company board where nobody outranks anyone
setter's reading: a board is also a piece of furniture, here the legendary one at which King Arthur's knights sat with no head place

explanation.walkthrough: Board looks like a committee, but it is the wooden surface; Arthur's knights sat around it so none could claim precedence.
explanation.definitionFit: The circular piece of furniture at Camelot had no head seat, so every knight sat as a peer of the others.

clue.text: Avoided having a mini, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: went around a problem rather than facing it
second meaning: wearing a short piece of clothing below the waist

explanation.walkthrough: A mini could be a car, but here it is a miniskirt, and 'perhaps' warns that it is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt an issue is to go around its edge, and someone wearing a skirt, such as a miniskirt, is skirted.

clue.text: Rustic bug mostly precedes abdominal pain

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
precedes puts the shortened word in front of what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
colic is severe pain in the abdomen

explanation.surface: A country illness: a tummy bug coming before stomach cramps.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucolic describes the countryside and shepherds' life, so it is a literary synonym for rural.

clue.text: PR getting into shape clumsily, maybe

indicators.note: doing something clumsily means it comes out disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A public relations firm getting fit, awkwardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting into' suggests putting PR inside, but the P and R end up apart, so all seven letters are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: Perhaps and maybe are interchangeable adverbs expressing possibility rather than certainty.

clue.text: Miss pal having wild fling with rider

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so the letters run in a disordered way

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman enjoying a passionate affair with a jockey.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss is a title for a young woman, so a Miss who is a companion is a female friend.

clue.text: Worry about being taken in by short measure

indicators.note: taken in by means held within, so the first piece sits inside the second

blocks.note: FT is the short form of foot, a unit of length
re means concerning

explanation.surface: Fretting about being shortchanged at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Short measure suggests a stingy pour; here it means an abbreviated unit.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret is to be anxious and agitated, so it serves as a verb synonym of worry.

clue.text: Scrap engagement?

blocks.note: first meaning: a brief fight
second meaning: a military encounter between forces

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests calling off a betrothal; scrap is a fight and engagement a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A skirmish is a minor fight between small groups, which fits both a brawl and a minor military clash.

clue.text: Some say "Chin chin!" when they down a measure

indicators.note: some means a part of what follows, so the letters lie inside the quoted toast

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words of the toast

explanation.surface: Drinkers toast each other as they knock back a tot.
explanation.walkthrough: Chin chin is a British toast said before drinking; a measure looks like a dose of spirits but is the unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: An inch is an imperial unit of length, one twelfth of a foot, so it is a measure.

clue.text: Drunken sot follows everyone with shares

indicators.note: a drunken person staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order
follows puts the shuffled word after the next piece

blocks.note: everyone is all
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunk trails after everyone who owns shares.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to distribute portions, so allots and shares are matching third-person verbs for dividing out.

clue.text: Latitude for subject to imprison king

indicators.note: to imprison is to lock inside, so one piece is held within the other

blocks.note: a topic is a subject of discussion
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A subject is told to jail the monarch, with latitude to do it.
explanation.walkthrough: Latitude looks like freedom of action; here it is a geographical line.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropics of Cancer and Capricorn are named parallels on the globe, each a line of latitude.

clue.text: Rested one's head, when tablet due

blocks.note: a pill is a tablet of medicine
money due is owed

explanation.surface: Someone lay down to sleep when their medicine was due.
explanation.definitionFit: To be pillowed is to have the head laid on a cushion, the soft support used in bed.
